Flawed Decentralization: Subordinating uniform national protections to fragmented local forest plans abdicates statutory stewardship (Wyoming v. USDA, 661 F.3d 1209 (10th Cir. 2011)).

Given that the 2001 Rule was itself the product of extensive litigation — including a Ninth Circuit affirmation in *California ex rel. Lockyer v. USDA*, 575 F.3d 999 (9th Cir. 2009) — replacing a litigated national standard with 100+ discretionary, revisable local plans is likely to generate a comparable or greater volume of legal challenges, undermining the Department's stated goal of reducing administrative burden.

I am submitting this comment as an active American sportsman, angler, and hunter in formal opposition to the Forest Service’s proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), the National Forest Management Act (NFMA), 16 U.S.C. §§ 1600–1614, and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. § 4321 et seq. The Forest Service must withdraw this rule and preserve nationwide roadless protections.

In California ex rel. Lockyer v. USDA, 575 F.3d 999 (9th Cir. 2009), the Ninth Circuit struck down the 2005 State Petitions Rule because the agency failed to conduct a programmatic "hard look" at the cumulative environmental impacts of removing national protections.

It has survived extensive litigation, including affirmation by the Ninth Circuit in California ex rel. Lockyer v. U.S. Department of Agriculture, precisely because it reflects a durable, congressionally supported judgment that these lands merit protection from road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting.
Since 2001, I have witnessed the Roadless Rule—through centralized management and an extensive history of litigation—prove ineffective and costly.
The 2001 Roadless Rule was developed through extensive public input and has been upheld by courts (e.g., California ex rel. Lockyer v. U.S. Department of Agriculture, 575 F.3d 999 (9th Cir. 2009)).

The 2001 rule has been the legal backbone of that stewardship for roadless areas across the national forest system, and the case for rescinding it does not survive contact with the agency's own findings.
The Constitution's Property Clause, Article IV, Section 3, Clause 2, gives Congress broad authority over federal property.

The Property Clause gives Congress power over federal territory, and Kleppe v. New Mexico, 426 U.S. 529 (1976), reads that power expansively enough that a direct challenge to USDA's authority would likely fail.
The Property Clause in the US Constitution (Article IV, Section 3, clause 2) provides Congress the authority to acquire, dispose of, and manage federal property.

The last time the Forest Service tried to unwind roadless protections outside the ordinary forest-by-forest planning process — the 2005 State Petitions Rule — the Ninth Circuit vacated it for failing to adequately analyze the rule's environmental and species impacts under NEPA and the Endangered Species Act, and the 2001 Rule was reinstated.
The rule states future projects would still require site-specific NEPA compliance at the individual forest level.

This also isn't the first attempt to unwind roadless protections — the 2001 Rule survived exactly this kind of rollback once already, in litigation culminating in the Ninth Circuit's 2009 decision in (California ex rel. Lockyer v. USDA 575 F.3d 999).

USDA's rationale — that NFMA forest-level planning, not a national rule, is the right vehicle here — is the exact argument Wyoming made trying to kill this rule, and the exact argument the Tenth Circuit rejected in Wyoming v. USDA, 661 F.3d 1209 (10th Cir. 2011), holding nothing in NFMA "precludes national action on a conservation issue within the power of the Forest Service," and reinstating the Rule nationwide.

Under NEPA, the Forest Service must take a "hard look" at how rescinding the rule will cause severe cumulative impacts to carbon storage and climate resilience (NEPA, 42 U.S.C. §4321 et seq.).

When the Tenth Circuit upheld the 2001 Rule in Wyoming v. USDA, 661 F.3d 1209 (10th Cir. 2011), it recognized the agency’s extensive record showing that local, forest-by-forest planning had demonstrably failed to prevent the piecemeal degradation of roadless areas.
